The main contribution lies in the use of FRF combined with finite element simulations and inverse analysis to back-calculate the norm and phase angle of the complex modulus from the first resonance peak. Title: Comparison of the 3-dim linear viscoelastic behavior of asphalt mixes determined with tension-compression and dynamic tests
App Evidence: conventional-test comparison (Complex modulus (E*))
Meth Evidence: excitation source (IR); sensors (IR); boundary conditions (IR); vibration modes (IR); repetitions (IR); temperature (IR); methodological comment (IR)

Raw IdM: Numerical inverse analysis (FEM or other)
Rheo Purpose: Master curve construction, Comparison of results from different tests (e.g. between MWP tests and complex modulus tests)
ABK:
This study is highly relevant for the TC MWP scope for two main reasons. (i) First, it introduces an automatic impact device for the IR test, which improves the accuracy and repeatability of the measurements compared to manual impacts. (ii) Second, it presents an advanced inverse analysis procedure based on the linear viscoelastic 2S2P1D model. The material parameters were identified by optimizing the agreement between experimental and numerical FRFs. The optimization was performed separately for each temperature using the Matlab fminsearch function and ten points around the first resonance peak. Among the twelve model parameters, only six (E₀, k, δ, τₑ, C₁, and C₂) were optimized, while the remaining parameters were fixed using values obtained from cyclic tension-compression tests.

The main conclusion is that the IR and tension-compression (TC) tests provide consistent estimates of the complex modulus. However, IR measurements resulted in higher values of the complex modulus magnitude and lower phase angles than TC tests. The authors attribute these differences to the nonlinear behavior of asphalt mixtures, since IR tests are performed at significantly lower strain levels (0.1 um/m) than conventional tension-compression tests (50 um/m).
